_about: Pre/post concept test for Module 4 (homology modelling). 'answer' is the index of the correct option. Check the science before using with students.

options: Building a 3D model of a protein from its sequence using the known structure of a related protein as a template
Measuring the structure of a protein in the lab
Docking a drug into a protein
Predicting a drug's half-life
questions.why: Related proteins fold in similar ways, so a known structure can be used as a pattern for a protein whose structure is unknown.

questions.q: The basic idea behind homology modelling is that…
options: protein structure is conserved more than sequence during evolution
sequence is conserved more than structure
unrelated proteins share the same structure
all proteins have the same structure
questions.why: Sequences can drift a lot while the fold stays almost the same, so similar sequences mean similar 3D shapes.

questions.q: Roughly what sequence identity between target and template usually allows a reliable model?
options: Above about 40%
About 5%
Exactly 100% only
Any value works the same
questions.why: Above about 40% identity the models are usually reliable in the core. Between 30% and 40% you must be careful, and below 30% the alignment itself becomes unreliable.

questions.q: Which factor should you check when choosing between two templates with similar sequence identity?
options: Experimental resolution, coverage and whether it is in the right state
The length of the file name
The colour of the picture
The year the protein was named
questions.why: A higher-resolution structure that covers the whole target and is in the form you need makes a better template.

questions.q: Why is the sequence alignment of target and template so important?
options: Every residue is placed using the alignment, so alignment errors become structure errors
It decides the colour of the model
It is the last step and does not affect the model
It only affects the file size
questions.why: The model copies positions from the template through the alignment. A shifted alignment places the wrong residues in the wrong places.

questions.q: Where should gaps normally be placed in an alignment?
options: In loops, not inside helices or strands
Inside helices
Inside strands
Anywhere, it does not matter
questions.why: Helices and strands are the stable core. Loops tolerate insertions and deletions.

questions.q: A model's backbone angles all fall in the favoured Ramachandran regions. Does this prove the model is correct?
options: No. A wrong template or alignment can still give tidy angles
Yes, it proves the model is correct
Yes, but only for helices
It proves the alignment is perfect
questions.why: Copying a real backbone gives realistic angles even when it is the wrong protein. You must also check the template choice, the alignment and the environment of the residues.

questions.q: Which kind of residue is usually found buried in the core of a protein?
options: Hydrophobic residues such as leucine, isoleucine and valine
Charged residues such as aspartate and lysine
Water
Sugars
questions.why: Hydrophobic residues hide from water in the core. A charged residue buried in the core in a model is a warning sign.

questions.q: After building a model, what should you do before using it for docking or design?
options: Validate it (backbone angles, residue environment, comparison with other models) and think about its limits
Nothing, it is ready
Delete the template
Increase the resolution number
questions.why: Models contain errors. Validation shows where they are likely to be, and the binding site needs special care.

questions.q: What does a CA RMSD of 1.3 Å between a model and the true structure mean?
options: On average, the C-alpha atoms of the model are about 1.3 Å away from the true positions
The model is 1.3% correct
The model has 1.3 helices
The protein is 1.3 Å wide
questions.why: RMSD is the average distance (as a root mean square) between matching atoms after the best superposition. Smaller is better.
